title: Everyone is talking about the "great lock-in"
description:
January isn’t the only time for new year’s resolutions anymore. The end of the year is having a moment too - as part of the great lock-in trend. There’s lots of content online about locking in for the last four months of the year - whether that’s working out more regularly, spending less time on your phone, or trying to get that promotion at work.

Some people call it a winter arc, a September reset or the fresh-start effect - why have so many of us decided this is the perfect time for self-improvement? And is striving for optimisation all the time necessarily a good thing?

We hear from Adeja Shivonne, a lifestyle content creator based in New York City, who shares how her great lock-in is going. And BBC journalist Melissa Hogenboom explains what the science says about how to successfully set new goals - and stick to them.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討「 great lock-in 」年末自我提升潮流，以及如何讓目標轉化為持久的習慣。內容創作者 Adeja 分享減少早晨滑手機、運動與存錢的經驗，強調設定小而務實的目標，即使只完成一部分也有價值。 BBC 記者 Melissa Hogenboom 解釋「重新開始效應」：人們可以自行選擇有意義的時間點重新出發，不必等到新年。她建議將目標拆成可執行的日常行動，例如飯後散步，並提醒養成習慣的時間會因行為而異。面對社群媒體帶來的不斷自我優化壓力，節目鼓勵聽眾考慮長期的自己、設定可衡量的目標，並容許休息與偶爾未能堅持。
summaryEn: This episode explores the great lock-in trend of using the final months of the year for self-improvement. Content creator Adeja describes goals such as avoiding her phone in the morning, exercising, and saving money. She argues that small, realistic goals and partial progress are worthwhile. BBC journalist Melissa Hogenboom explains the fresh start effect and says people can choose a meaningful starting point rather than wait for January. She recommends turning goals into manageable daily habits, such as walking after dinner, and notes that the time needed to establish a habit varies. The discussion also considers the anxiety created by constant online self-optimization. Thinking about one's future self, making goals measurable, and allowing time for rest can help keep change purposeful and realistic.
